scenario: A school district's remediation program database contains only students who scored above 60 on the standardised mathematics assessment (students below 60 were referred to a separate support programme and are not tracked in this database). An analyst uses the database to estimate the district's average mathematics ability.

data.description: Only students with score > 60 appear in the remediation database. Scores assumed Normal with known standard deviation Ïƒ = 15.

question: The database shows a mean score of 68. Using the truncated normal model, estimate (a) the true population mean score Î¼ for all students in the district, and (b) the fraction of students whose scores appear in this database.
naive_answer: The true mean score is approximately 68, since that is the observed average.
naive_trap: The database only contains the top 17% of students. The observed mean of 68 is far above the true population mean of ~46. A policy maker using the database mean would dramatically overestimate district-wide mathematics ability.
reasoning_trace: Step 1: E[X|X>60] = Î¼ + 15Â·Î»((60-Î¼)/15) = 68. Step 2: Solve numerically for Î¼. The solution is Î¼ â‰ˆ 45.6. Step 3: Fraction in database = P(X>60 | Î¼=45.6, Ïƒ=15) = Î¦Ì„((60-45.6)/15) = Î¦Ì„(0.96) â‰ˆ 0.169.
python_verification:
from scipy.optimize import brentq
from scipy.stats import norm
def eq(mu): a=(60-mu)/15; sf=norm.sf(a); return mu+15*norm.pdf(a)/sf-68 if sf>1e-10 else 1e10
mu=brentq(eq,1,59.99)
assert abs(mu-45.61)<1.0
assert abs(norm.sf((60-mu)/15)-0.1687)<0.01
